vignette:
He is seventy years old, and when he walks into my office he moves like a man who has spent a lifetime bracing himself. He is compact, shoulders rounded, hands thick with calluses and white scars from the welding torch. He sits on the edge of the chair, never letting his back touch the cushion. His eyes scan the room in a steady, practiced rhythm—door, window, corner, me—then back again. He holds a small leather wallet in both hands, turning it over and over, the way some men worry a rosary.

It started forty-two years ago, in a small city in the highlands of his home country. He was a welder then too, working for a construction company that built bridges and culverts. He had joined a local union council, not out of politics, he says, but because the men needed someone to keep the ledger and speak to the foreman. The new government saw that as subversion. One evening he was walking home from the shop, his welding helmet still hooked to his belt, when three men in civilian clothes pulled him into a black sedan.

He tells me he does not remember the first week. Only the smell. The smell of burning metal, but different—wrong. Not steel, not flux, but flesh. After that, the days collapse into a single heavy moment that keeps happening over and over. He was hung from a steel pipe by his wrists, and his shoulders still ache when the weather shifts. He was shocked with wires attached to his hands—the same hands that could lay a clean bead of weld down a joint of pipe. He was made to kneel for hours on a concrete floor, and his knees remain stiff and sore, though he never mentions it unless I ask.

He escaped after three months. A guard opened the door and looked away. He ran, barefoot, across fields and through dry riverbeds until he reached the border. He made his way north to the United States, and for years he worked in welding shops in Texas and California. He married a woman from his hometown who had also fled. They had three children, now grown, scattered across the country. She died eight years ago—cancer. He still sleeps on his side of the bed.

Now he works part-time at a small fabrication shop. He can still weld, but he has to stop sometimes. Certain sounds undo him. The hiss of a torch triggering a flashback. The clang of a dropped pipe makes him drop to the ground before he knows what he is doing. The owner of the shop, a young man, is patient. He lets him take breaks.

At home he cannot sit still. He cleans the kitchen counters obsessively, then goes out to the garage and organizes his tools. He has not turned on the television in three years because the news anchors’ voices remind him of the interrogations. He avoids crowds, even grocery stores. He eats the same meal every night—rice, beans, a piece of chicken—because it feels safe. He sleeps in short, restless bursts, often waking at three in the morning with his heart hammering, convinced he hears footsteps in the hallway.

He tells me he does not feel much anymore. Not anger, not sadness, not joy. Just a low simmering vigilance, like a pilot light that never goes out. When his daughter calls, he lets the voicemail answer, then listens to her message three times before calling back. He wonders if he is a burden. He wonders if he ever really left that room with the pipe and the wires.

He came to see me because his doctor told him his blood pressure was dangerous. But what he really wants, I think, is to know if there is a day coming when he can stop looking over his shoulder. He does not say this. He just holds the wallet and watches the door.
